questions.q: Why does this lesson say keeping secrets out of Apex code via Named Credentials doesn't automatically mean they're fully locked down?
options: Because the governance question of who can view or edit the Named Credential setup records themselves is separate from whether the pattern (Named Credential vs. hardcoded secret) was followed
Because Named Credentials cannot store authentication details at all
Because Apex code is always more secure than any setup record
Because Named Credentials automatically expire after 24 hours
questions.explain: A Named Credential being out of code is necessary but not sufficient -- if too many users have edit access to the setup area holding it, the discipline is undermined by a separate, unaddressed permissions gap.

questions.q: What does Shield Platform Encryption add on top of field-level security and sharing?
options: It replaces the need for field-level security entirely
It automatically grants Event Monitoring access to all users
It is only relevant for Named Credential configuration, not actual data fields
It encrypts specific field values at rest, protecting against exposure from the raw storage layer, which is a different threat than controlling who can query the field through the application
questions.explain: Field-level security and sharing control application-layer query access; Shield Platform Encryption separately protects against someone reading plaintext directly from underlying storage -- the two are complementary, not substitutes for each other.

questions.q: What question does Event Monitoring help answer that access controls like sharing sets and External ID matching do not?
options: Whether a record can be accessed at all
Which fields are marked as External ID
Whether, after the fact, unusual activity (like an integration user exporting far more data than normal) can actually be detected
Whether a Named Credential uses OAuth or Basic authentication
questions.explain: Access controls answer 'can this happen'; Event Monitoring answers 'if this happens, do we know about it' -- a distinct, complementary governance question.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the security/governance review (Lesson 16) and the design-comparison review (Lesson 15) as orthogonal rather than redundant?
options: Because they ask entirely unrelated questions about different course topics with no shared subject matter
Because they run different lenses (volume/latency/failure-risk vs. secrets/access/visibility) over the same five case studies, each surfacing considerations the other doesn't
Because Lesson 16 replaces everything taught in Lesson 15
Because only one of the two lessons applies to real review boards
questions.explain: Both lessons revisit the same five case studies but ask different kinds of questions -- a real review typically needs both passes, since neither lens surfaces everything the other one does.

questions.q: What specific risk does the lesson flag regarding the CRM+Data Warehouse integration's integration user?
options: That a compromised or misconfigured integration user quietly exporting far more data than its normal job requires would only ever be caught by watching an event log, not by trusting the access controls were configured correctly
That the integration user cannot technically authenticate to Salesforce
That data warehouses are incapable of receiving any Salesforce data via API
That Named Credentials cannot be used for integration users, only human users
questions.explain: Access controls alone don't catch an authorized-but-abused account; detecting an unusual spike in that account's activity depends on actually monitoring the event log.
